clinicalPearls: Scaphoid nonunion typically follows a missed, inadequately immobilised or displaced waist fracture, and the retrograde blood supply predisposes the proximal pole to avascular necrosis.
The blood supply enters distally via dorsal ridge branches of the radial artery, so more proximal fractures heal least reliably.
Untreated nonunion produces a humpback (flexion) deformity with a DISI posture and a predictable arthritic cascade termed SNAC.
SNAC progresses from radial styloid and distal scaphoid arthritis to periscaphoid and midcarpal degeneration, characteristically sparing the radiolunate joint.
CT reconstructed along the long axis of the scaphoid best defines union, displacement and humpback deformity.
MRI assesses proximal pole vascularity and helps decide between vascularised and non-vascularised bone grafting.
Vascularised bone grafting is favoured for an avascular proximal pole, whereas structural wedge grafting is used to correct humpback deformity.
reference.pathophysiology: The scaphoid is largely covered by articular cartilage and receives most of its blood supply retrogradely from branches of the radial artery entering the distal dorsal ridge. A fracture, particularly of the waist or proximal pole, can devascularise the proximal fragment. Persistent motion combined with poor vascularity prevents bridging bone and produces a fibrous or sclerotic nonunion. Volar bone resorption causes the scaphoid to collapse into flexion, the humpback deformity, with compensatory lunate extension producing DISI. Altered load transmission then drives progressive periscaphoid and midcarpal arthritis, the SNAC pattern.
additionalInvestigations: PA, lateral, oblique and dedicated scaphoid-view radiographs
CT reconstructed along the scaphoid long axis for union and deformity assessment
MRI to evaluate proximal pole vascularity
Intraoperative assessment of punctate bleeding to gauge bone vascularity
Metabolic or inflammatory screen in atypical presentations
redFlags: Proximal pole sclerosis or fragmentation indicating avascular necrosis
Radiographic SNAC changes signalling irreversible arthritis
Persistent wrist pain and functional decline in a young manual worker
reference.prognosis: With appropriate grafting and fixation before arthritis develops, union rates are good, but established SNAC arthritis is irreversible and ultimately requires salvage surgery.
pitfalls: Missing the original fracture on initial radiographs and mislabelling it a sprain.
Assuming union on plain films without CT confirmation.
Neglecting proximal pole vascularity assessment before selecting a graft.
Failing to correct humpback deformity and leaving residual malalignment.
Overlooking established SNAC arthritis when planning reconstruction.
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
